title: Bidirectional BFS in Berlin: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch two BFS frontiers race from start and goal across Berlin’s street-grid at the same time. When they meet, you reconstruct the path—cutting the search space dramatically for faster routing.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

In this Berlin (Mitte) grid simulation, instead of exploring outward from the start only, we run BFS from:
1) Start → expanding layer-by-layer
2) Goal → expanding layer-by-layer

The “meeting in the middle” moment is the key optimization: once the two visited regions touch, you stop searching and stitch the path from both sides. Think of it like searching a maze from both ends—each side only needs to travel ~√N steps instead of N in many cases, shrinking the work massively.

Technical takeaway (interview-level):
- Unweighted graphs → BFS guarantees shortest paths.
- Maintain two queues + two visited maps (parent pointers).
- Stop when a node appears in both visited sets; reconstruct using stored parents.

Debate question: In your experience, when does bidirectional BFS *not* beat classic BFS (e.g., directed graphs, unbalanced branching factors, or expensive neighbor generation)?
